research.lane: Code graphs built for coding agents (repository maps, research localisation systems, symbol-index and MCP tools, builder statements). Today 2026-11-12. All numbers are authors' own as seen through a page-to-markdown fetch tool; "fetched" means read via that tool (extraction, sometimes truncated), not a human read. No experiment run, nothing installed, repo untouched.

findings.claim: Aider's repo map: file-level graph, personalised PageRank, token-budgeted output; no published ablation of the map
findings.detail: Nodes = files; edge referencer->definer per identifier that is both defined and referenced (multigraph, self-edge 0.1 for unreferenced defs). Tree-sitter tags cached per file by mtime. Edge weight = multiplier*sqrt(ref count); multipliers: identifier mentioned in chat x10, long snake/camel/kebab name (8+ chars) x10, leading underscore x0.1, more than 5 definers x0.1, referencing file in chat x50. Personalisation on chat files and files whose names match mentioned identifiers. Output = paths + ranked definition lines (signatures), binary-searched to a token budget (default 1,024; up to 8x when no files in chat, capped by context window minus 4,096). No hop limit (global PageRank). The 2023 blog reports no benchmark; the 2024 SWE-bench Lite post reports 70.3 % correct-file pick and 26.3 % pass@1 (79/300) but no with/without-map comparison. Searches found no third-party ablation.

findings.claim: RepoGraph: 1-hop ego-graph helps modestly; 2-hop flattened is worse than no graph and costs 4x the tokens
findings.detail: Line-level def/ref nodes, contain/invoke edges, tree-sitter, Python only. SWE-bench Lite (300): Agentless(GPT-4o) 27.33->29.67 %, AutoCodeRover(GPT-4) 19.00->21.33, SWE-agent(GPT-4o) 18.33->20.33, RAG(GPT-4) 2.67->5.33; tokens rose in every case (Agentless 42,376->47,323; SWE-agent 498,346->518,792). File localisation +4 to +6.7 pts, line +1.6 to +2.7. Hop ablation (Agentless): 1-hop flatten 29.67 % at 2,311 tokens; 1-hop summary 28.33 % at 718; 2-hop flatten 26.00 % (below 27.33 baseline) at 10,505; 2-hop summary 28.67 % at 1,229. Only GPT-4-family in main runs, Lite only, Python only, k stops at 2.

findings.claim: CodexGraph (Neo4j + LLM-written Cypher) used more tokens than AutoCodeRover and collapsed on weaker models
findings.detail: Python schema (MODULE/CLASS/METHOD/FUNCTION/FIELD/GLOBAL_VARIABLE; CONTAINS/HAS_METHOD/HAS_FIELD/INHERITS/USES; no call edges). GPT-4o: CrossCodeEval EM 27.9 vs BM25 21.2; EvoCodeBench Pass@1 36.02 vs 28.78 (AutoCodeRover); SWE-bench Lite (257 of 300 evaluated, 43 sympy tasks dropped for OOM at indexing) 22.96 = AutoCodeRover 22.96. Tokens per SWE-bench sample: BM25 14.76k, AutoCodeRover 76.01k, CodexGraph 102.25k. Qwen2-72B SWE-bench 1.95 % vs AutoCodeRover 9.34 %. Removing the Cypher-translation agent drops CrossCodeEval EM 27.90 -> 8.30.

findings.claim: LocAgent: lexical entry point is worth far more than graph traversal in its own ablation
findings.detail: Nodes dir/file/class/function; edges contain/import/invoke/inherit; Python only; AST index in seconds; 4-layer sparse index (qualified id, short-name dict, BM25 over ids, chunk inverted index). Tools SearchEntity, TraverseGraph (typed BFS, hops configurable), RetrieveEntity. Lite, Claude-3.5: file Acc@5 94.16, function Acc@10 77.37 vs Agentless 79.56/58.76, OpenHands 90.15/70.07, BM25 61.68/36.86, CodeRankEmbed 84.67/58.76; fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32B 92.70/77.01 at $0.09/instance vs $0.46-0.83 for agents. Ablation (7B ft; file Acc@5/module Acc@10/function Acc@10): full 88.32/82.85/71.53; no TraverseGraph 86.13/78.47/66.06; hops fixed 1: 86.86/80.29/66.79; only contain edges 86.50/79.56/66.42; no SearchEntity 68.98/61.31/53.28; no BM25 index 75.18/68.98/60.22. Downstream with Agentless editor Pass@1 26.31->27.92. Third-party reproductions give LocAgent much lower numbers (CoSIL: function Top-1 0.103 on Lite with Qwen2.5-32B, 13.67 % empty; GREPO Hit@1 5.04), different harnesses.

findings.claim: CoSIL: run-time LLM-built first-order graphs, one hop per iteration with a pruner, beat other localisers on function Top-1 at low token cost, but iteration count is non-monotonic
findings.detail: Module graph (import) then function graph (invoke/inherit), built by the LLM per query, no index, max 10 iterations, pruner call per node. Qwen2.5-Coder-32B function Top-1: Lite 0.433 vs Agentless-FL 0.247, OrcaLoca 0.217, LocAgent 0.103; Verified 0.446 vs 0.326/0.254/0.250. File Top-1 Lite 0.613 below LocAgent 0.647. Cost on 50-instance subset: about 0.07M tokens/$0.022 (DeepSeek-V3), about 0.14M/$0.34 (GPT-4o; LocAgent about $4.00). Ablation (function Top-1): no iteration 0.320, no module graph 0.383, no reflection 0.390, no pruner 0.413. Iteration sweep 0.383 (1), 0.347 (3), 0.430 (10). Python only; ablation on one model; paper's headline numbers inconsistent (48 % / 65 % / 43.3 %).

findings.claim: OrcaLoca: call-and-containment graph with shortest-path context pruning; large localisation numbers but Python and Claude only
findings.detail: Entity + directory nodes, AST containment edges, AST function-call edges only (no imports/variable refs). Heap scheduler, relevance-scoring sub-agent, pruning by mean min forward/reverse shortest-path distance to candidate locations, top 12 entries. Lite (Claude-3.5-Sonnet): function match 65.33 %, file 83.33 %, resolved 41.00 %; about $0.87 search + $0.90 repair per instance; +6.67 pts function match and +6.33 resolved over reproduced Agentless. Ablations (93 instances) 1.1-5.4 pts each. Last 11.8k characters unread.

findings.claim: Non-graph comparisons are strong: Agentless (no graph) 32.00 % Lite at $0.70; AutoCodeRover 19 % at $0.43 using AST search APIs not a graph
findings.detail: Agentless: LLM over repo tree, embedding retrieval, file skeletons, edit locations; file 69.7 %, function 52.0 %, line 35.3 %; authors say agents beat it when the issue gives no location clue. 4.3 % of Lite issues contain the gold patch, about 10 % lack enough information. AutoCodeRover: stratified class/method/snippet search over AST, GPT-4, 195 s, $0.43; of unresolved 29 % had correct locations but a wrong patch, 18 % wrong file. Agentless last 24k characters unread.

findings.claim: Parser-built deterministic graphs beat LLM-built graphs on cost and coverage; evidence is Java, 3 repos, 15 questions each, single annotator
findings.detail: Shopizer (1,210 files): correct/partial/incorrect 15/0/0 deterministic tree-sitter graph (nodes = types; injects/extends/implements; bidirectional traversal), 13/2/0 LLM-extracted graph, 6/4/5 vector-only. Index time 22.09 s vs 215.09 s vs 18.41 s; cost $0.09 / $0.79 / $0.04. Over 45 questions 43/38/31 correct. LLM extractor skipped 377 of 1,210 files. Depth d not visible; one representative run, no confidence intervals; last 25k characters unread.

findings.claim: With a frontier agent (Claude Code, Haiku 4.5), five map-based MCP servers cut tokens 17-39 % and left task success about unchanged
findings.detail: Servers: AST skeleton, call graph (Jedi for Python, name-matched C/C++), file import graph, docs (BM25, no graph), hybrid. Query path: FTS5 BM25 seeds -> expansion along edges -> random-walk-with-restart ranking -> top snippets grouped by file with relation lines. LinuxFLBench n=152: file recall@10 0.717 baseline vs 0.757-0.829 (hybrid best); tokens 1,008,163 -> 610,910-754,768 (-25 to -39 %). SWE-bench Pro n=253: resolved 49.0 % vs AST 50.6, callgraph 46.2, deps 49.4, docs 44.3, hybrid 50.6; tokens -17 to -26 %. SecBench: callgraph 34.3 % vs 28.9. SWT-bench: tokens and latency up for all. One run per task, no significance tests, hop/depth not stated, repo sizes not reported; repair runs add a hook forcing one map query, confounding representation and steering.

findings.claim: Codebase-Memory (SQLite property graph over MCP): about 10x fewer tokens per question than grep-and-read, at 0.83 vs 0.92 answer quality
findings.detail: 12 node types; edges incl. CALLS, HTTP_CALLS, ASYNC_CALLS, IMPORTS, IMPLEMENTS, INHERITS, TESTS; tree-sitter, 66 grammars; Louvain communities; 6-strategy call resolution with confidence; XXH3 incremental sync (about 1.2 s re-index); BFS via SQL recursive CTE; 14 MCP tools; stores no source lines. Django 49,398 nodes/196,022 edges, about 6 s to index. Claude Opus 4.6 both arms: about 1,000 vs 10,000 tokens/question, 2.3 vs 4.8 tool calls. Graph arm won hub detection and caller ranking in 19 of 31 languages; explorer won full source context (16/31) and exhaustive grep (10/31); macro-heavy C 0.58 vs 1.00. Weaknesses: one repo per language (smallest 78 nodes), first author grades, question count unstated, no embedding or LSP baseline, indexing cost not counted in tokens.

findings.claim: Graph at repair stage hurts; only localisation use helps (SeeRepo)
findings.detail: AST graph (files/classes/functions; contains/imports/inherits/invokes) rendered as Graphviz image from BFS of given depth. SWE-bench Verified: GPT-5-mini 55.0->55.4 % with input tokens -25 %; GPT-5.1 51.0->48.8 % with cost -46 %; Kimi K2.5 68.8->70.6 % with tokens +5 %; Doubao 51.0->52.0 %, tokens -4.8 %. Used at repair stage: -5.0 pts; at patch validation -3.4; depth 1: -0.6; vision-only -13.6 to -34.1 pts and cost up to +268 %. Python only.

findings.claim: Hop depth: agents rarely chain graph expansions, and accuracy about halves per extra hop; graph tools help most at hop 0-1 and with small models
findings.detail: SWE-bench Verified, 10 models 0.6B-32B, about 79k episodes, primary 160 depth-balanced tasks (about +/-5 pts). Tasks by hop distance from issue-mentioned code to patched code: 186 at hop 0, 128 at 1, 78 at 2, 76 at 3+. Each extra hop multiplies odds of correct function localisation by 0.47-0.55 (four models). Graph tools roughly double grep-only 8B accuracy (12.8 % -> 24-30 %), about +8 pts at 4B, only +4-5 at 32B (tool uptake falls: find_entity called in 96 % of episodes at 14B, 45 % at 32B). Agents chain expansions in 12-14 % of episodes. Embeddings added nothing at 4B (-1.1). From 8B up about half the gain comes from submitting exact entity ids. Repair with these localisations: 6/13/12/13 of 160 (grep/emb/graph/both) vs oracle 26. Graphs averaged about 26,000 nodes and 233,000 edges. Same graph used for hop labels and tools; small models; one language.

findings.claim: LARGER: sidecar graph anchored on the agent's own lexical search; typed edges, confidence and expansion each carry measurable value; no hop sweep seen
findings.detail: Heterogeneous graph (dir/file/class/function; contains/imports/invokes plus source-to-test and source-to-doc), multi-language AST, edge confidence threshold 0.5, K-hop expansion up to 10 neighbours by score, Leiden communities as prior; not PageRank. Incremental by re-parsing changed files. LocBench file Acc@5 87.0 vs Claude Code 75.2, Codex 74.1 (only 374 of 560 instances completed); MuLocBench Acc@5 55.7 vs 54.9 / 50.0, but Claude Code leads Acc@1 29.2 vs 27.4. Tokens 353k vs Codex 522k per instance, 99.9 s vs 139.9 s. Ablation MuLocBench Acc@5 (full 55.7): no expansion 48.2, no confidence 53.1, no communities 53.4, no graph modules 46.8. In-house methods GPT-5.2, Claude Code Opus 4.6 (backbones differ). Last 29k characters unread.

findings.claim: ARISE: statement-level data-flow graph raised pass@1 but added tokens and a very long build; coarse graph matched it
findings.detail: Typed property graph with statement nodes and def-use edges (Python ast, intra-procedural); tools incl. bounded-BFS data-flow slice and a context bundle capped at 8,000 tokens. Qwen2.5-Coder-32B in SWE-agent, Lite pass@1 17.3 -> 22.0 %; function R@1 0.43->0.60; tokens 510k -> 560k (about 3,200 extra tokens per extra resolved instance). Median graph 134k nodes/313k edges; first build 1.7 s (requests) to 33 min (sympy). ARISE-Coarse within 0.01 of Structural. On Qwen3.6-35B: SWE-agent 33.3->34.0, AutoCodeRover 36.3->32.0. Single run.

findings.claim: Strong non-graph localisers: bash-only RL agent (CodeScout), parallel grep subagents (SWE-grep, FastContext)
findings.detail: CodeScout (1.7B/4B/14B, bash only, no graph): Verified file/function F1 14B 68.57/40.32 vs RepoNavigator-32B 67.75/34.09; Pro 14B 53.63/28.74 vs RepoNavigator-32B 57.57/20.72; Lite 14B 71.84/44.43; no same-agent ablation of graph vs bash; baseline numbers copied from papers. FastContext: reading+searching = 56.2 % of tool-use turns and 46.5 % of tokens in GPT-5.4 trajectories; explorer subagent raises SWE-bench Pro GPT-5.4 46.0->51.5 % and cuts main-agent tokens up to 60.3 % (SWE-QA). SWE-grep: 4 turns x 8 parallel calls, weighted F1 beta 0.5 (precision favoured because polluting context hurt more than omitting), no numeric F1 in the extracted text.

findings.claim: Builder statements: Claude Code dropped its index for agentic grep; Cursor reports index gains concentrated in 1,000+ file repos; Augment reports -30 % tokens with parity quality
findings.detail: Cherny (Latent Space): early index+retrieval replaced by glob/grep agentic search, 'outperformed by a lot' on internal vibes and some internal benchmarks, reasons drift/security/simplicity, cost = latency and tokens; no numbers. Anthropic context-engineering post: just-in-time retrieval, CLAUDE.md up front; slower than pre-computed retrieval. Cursor (2025-11-06): own embedding model; Context Bench +12.5 % (6.5-23.5 % by model); online code retention +0.3 % overall, +2.6 % at 1,000+ files; best with grep alongside. Cline (2025-05): no measurements. Cody: moved enterprise off embeddings, no data (snippet only). Augment (2026-05/06): SWE-Bench Pro 61.8 vs 59.9 %, tokens -30 %, cost -23 %; Terminal Bench 2.0 67.4 vs 66.3 % (vendor says inside run variance), tokens -32 %; private suite 72.6 vs 73.8 %, cost per pass -40 %; task counts and repo sizes unstated, vendor-run.

findings.claim: Repository overview files do not help agent success and add cost; test-linking graph cuts regressions on small local models
findings.detail: AGENTS.md study: context files do not generally improve success and raise inference cost over 20 % on average; repository overviews not helpful, instructions followed (abstract only). TDAD (code-to-test graph, naming/directory test links, NetworkX): Qwen3-Coder 30B, 100 Verified tasks, test-level regression 6.08 -> 1.82 % but resolution 31 -> 29 %; second phase 25 tasks 24 -> 32 %; shortening the skill file 107 -> 20 lines moved resolution 12 -> 50 % on 10 tasks; no token data; 11 of 15 auto-loop iterations reverted.

findings.claim: Language-server and symbol-index tools: documented capability, no agent token or accuracy measurement found
findings.detail: Claude Code LSP tool: needs a per-language plugin plus a user-installed server binary (pyright, typescript-language-server in the official table); definition, references, call hierarchy, diagnostics after edits; inactive in cloud sessions; docs warn of high memory while indexing and false unresolved imports in monorepos; community bug report of definition/references returning empty while hover works (snippet). SCIP: protobuf index (documents, occurrences, string symbols), per-language indexers incl. scip-python and scip-typescript, replaced LSIF, compresses to 10-20 %; no agent evaluation. github/stack-graphs archived read-only 2025-09-09.

findings.claim: No paper compares a graph database with a relational store holding the same edges; engine is never the variable
findings.detail: Neo4j appears only in CodexGraph (OOM on sympy, high tokens). Working systems use SQLite with recursive CTE (Codebase-Memory), NetworkX (Aider, TDAD, the Java graph-RAG study), cached in-process graphs (ARISE), a sidecar index (LARGER). What the literature varies is graph content, ranking, hop limit, return format and cap. The owner's point that the test must separate engine from structure and ranking is supported by the absence of any such control.
findings.source: synthesis of CodexGraph, Codebase-Memory, Aider, TDAD, ARISE, LARGER

recommendations_for_the_build: Build the graph deterministically with parsers (tree-sitter for Python, JS/JSX, TS; Python ast or Jedi-class resolution and the TypeScript compiler API already in technician-app/node_modules/typescript for call resolution). Evidence: parser graphs beat LLM graphs on cost and coverage; all positive localisation systems except CoSIL use AST extraction.

Use few typed edges with a confidence value on each: contains, imports, calls, inherits, tests, documents (doc cites file or symbol), plus repo-specific HTTP edges (client URL literal -> route decorator) and a same-name-slice link across runtimes. Typed and confidence-weighted edges and source-to-test/doc edges have ablation support (LARGER); cross-runtime edges have no measured support, only shipped tools (Codebase-Memory HTTP_CALLS), so build them as a separately switchable edge class.

Make the entry point lexical: BM25/FTS over symbol names, paths, docstrings and doc text picks seeds. LocAgent ablation: removing SearchEntity costs 19 points file Acc@5, removing TraverseGraph about 2. Add exact-name resolution (find_entity style) as the first tool.

Expand 1 hop by default, up to 2 only through a ranked, capped result; rank the neighbourhood with personalised PageRank or random walk with restart (Aider, 2611.07286); cap output in tokens (Aider 1,024 up to 8x; ARISE 8,000; small-agent tool 50 edges); return paths, signatures, line ranges and relation lines, not source bodies; favour precision over recall (Cognition).

Expose it as a few on-demand tools beside grep and read, not as a standing prompt overview (2611.07286 mounts tools beside native ones; AGENTS.md study: overviews gave no success gain and over 20 % more cost).
Update incrementally by per-file hash or mtime (Aider, Codebase-Memory about 1.2 s). At 477 code files a full rebuild is seconds, so caching is about freshness.

Store in the simplest in-process form (SQLite + recursive CTE, or an in-memory graph library). The literature gives no support for a graph database server at this size, and none against either; keep the engine swappable so the test can vary it.
Target localisation and impact analysis (which files, tests, callers), not the edit step (SeeRepo repair -5.0, validation -3.4 pts).
Do NOT use: LLM-written Cypher, LLM-extracted graphs, raw 2-hop dumps, statement-level data-flow graphs, image-rendered graphs, trained graph models (CGM, GNN).
recommendations_for_the_test: Separate the engine from the structure: store identical edges and run the identical ranking and hop logic in a relational table (recursive CTEs) and in a graph structure; then vary content, ranking, hops, cap and return format independently. No paper does this.

Score the answer and its value, not the store size: gold-location recall@k and precision against files a fix commit actually changed (Loc-Bench-style, from the repo's own history: 72 fix commits, 368 on main), tokens returned, steps to first correct file, and downstream task success; report per-hop-distance strata (small-agent study method) because averages hide the hop-0/1 vs hop-2+ split.

Baselines: grep+read only; BM25 symbol search; an Aider-style ranked map at 1k and 8k tokens; graph with 0, 1, 2, 3 hops each with and without ranking and with and without a token cap; add HTTP/test/doc edge classes one at a time.
Hold model and agent harness constant across arms (LARGER and Augment comparisons change backbones; those are not usable as a pattern). Use the model the owner actually runs.

Repeat each condition several times; treat differences under about 3 to 5 points as noise at 100-300 task scale (small-agent study; Augment states 1.1 pts is run variance; most 2026 papers use one run).
Include task types where localisation is not the bottleneck (editing, test writing) to see the null or negative cases (2611.07286 SWT-bench tokens up; SeeRepo repair -5.0).
Count build, update and tool-description tokens in the cost (2611.07286 omits map-construction cost; Codebase-Memory excludes indexing).
open_questions: Does a cross-runtime HTTP edge (client URL literal to route decorator, about 73 literals vs 77 routes here) reduce steps or raise localisation on tasks that span web/mobile and backend? Tools ship it; no paper measures it.
At roughly 500 code files, where is the break-even between grep-plus-read and any index? Only Cursor gives a size-stratified signal (+0.3 % overall, +2.6 % at 1,000+ files).
Is the engine (graph database vs relational) ever the variable that matters once content, ranking and output format are fixed? No source tests it.
Does ranked 2-3 hop closure computed by the tool beat leaving chaining to the model? The small-agent paper suggests it but did not test it; no hop sweep beyond 2 with ranking exists.
Do tool-returned graph results help frontier models on accuracy at all, or only on tokens? Existing frontier-model evidence (2611.07286, SeeRepo, Augment) shows tokens down and success about flat.

How much does steering (a hook forcing one map query, a short skill file) contribute versus the graph itself? 2611.07286 and TDAD (107 to 20 line skill file moved resolution 12 to 50 % on 10 tasks) both confound them.

findings.detail: Kuzu repo archived 2025-10-10, last release 0.11.3, MIT. LadybugDB (MIT) PyPI 0.22.3 released 2026-11-06 (0.19.1 was the latest in an Aug 2026 post, so about 3 minor versions in 3 months). GitHub: ~1.9k stars, 6,942 commits on main. findings.claim: LadybugDB's Cypher covers variable-length, shortest and weighted-shortest paths with selectable path modes and in-path predicates
findings.detail: *min..max default max 30; WALK is the default, TRAIL (distinct edges) and ACYCLIC (distinct nodes) are options; SHORTEST (one per endpoint), ALL SHORTEST, WSHORTEST(prop), ALL WSHORTEST; in-path predicates (r, n | WHERE ...) limited to node-only, edge-only or AND-combinations; projection {r.prop} reduces memory.

findings.claim: PostgreSQL SQL/PGQ was reverted before the PostgreSQL 19 release, so the project's production engine has no native property-graph syntax
findings.detail: SQL/PGQ (GRAPH_TABLE) committed 2026-03-16 (commit 2f094e7ac69); reverted from master 2026-09-07 (commit b1f106c80cbeb18d3a0219994d98a51a6eca8ede, 49 commits, 124 files, no reason in the message). A later article says it was absent from beta 4 (2026-09-24) and RC1 (2026-10-15); beta-era articles that present it as shipping are outdated. PG19 GA and release notes not confirmed. Postgres still has recursive CTEs with CYCLE and SEARCH clauses. Apache AGE 1.8.0 (2026-08-11) targets PG18 only and has no official Windows build (Linux/Docker).
findings.source: postgresql.org/message-id/E1x3f62-00000003sxD-0vdk@gemulon.postgresql.org (2026-09-07); postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-with.html; search snippets for AGE and beta 4

findings.claim: DuckDB 2.0.0 (2026-10-21) plus the DuckPGQ community extension is a relational engine with graph syntax and algorithms, and is the best overall performer in one 2026 benchmark
findings.detail: DuckPGQ: SQL/PGQ GRAPH_TABLE, {1,3} quantifiers, ANY SHORTEST (non-deterministic on ties, no ALL paths), PageRank, WCC, local clustering coefficient; CSR built on the fly per query by UDFs; on 2.0 requires SET active_grammar_extensions=['duckpgq']; community page matrix lists 1.4.4 to 2.0.0 incl. Windows but cells blank; one doc mentions a csr_cte error. pip wheel 15.4 MB; npm @duckdb/node-api 2.0.0-r.1 plus win32-x64 binding 62.9 MB unpacked. DuckDB recursive CTEs gained USING KEY (1.3) and UNION semantics change in 2.0.

findings.claim: Same nodes, edges and 'same query' do not give the same answer unless path mode, output shape and tie rules are pinned
findings.detail: Neo4j and Memgraph enforce trail semantics (no repeated edge) during matching; Kuzu, DuckDB and a commercial RDBMS use walk and filter to trails afterwards (arXiv 2604.02553). Ladybug defaults to WALK. AGE enforces edge-uniqueness and returns every path, while a recursive CTE with UNION returns de-duplicated node ids; an AGE maintainer states they answer different questions. DuckPGQ offers only ANY SHORTEST. Reachability as a set of nodes is the case where SQL set semantics, CSR BFS and Cypher agree (my local test: identical counts in every cell; MetaQA test: identical candidate sets).
findings.source: arxiv.org/html/2604.02553v2; mid.mail-archive.com/dev@age.apache.org/msg08100.html and msg08106.html; docs.ladybugdb.com match page; local bench

findings.claim: Published storage sizes for the same data: relational stores were smaller than the native graph store; no source shows a graph store smaller than a well-tuned relational one for bare edges
findings.detail: Pacaci et al. 2017 SNB SF3 (3 GB raw): Neo4j 20 GB, Postgres 11 GB, Virtuoso-RDBMS 2.4 GB, Titan-C 6.3 GB, Virtuoso-RDF 8.5 GB; SF10 (10 GB raw): Neo4j 65, Postgres 36, Virtuoso 7, Titan-C 18. LOCAL: 5M edges, SQLite WITHOUT ROWID composite-key table 65.1 MB vs forward-only CSR 24.0 MB (2.7x); 500k edges 6.04 MB vs 2.40 MB. Joern flatgraph (custom code-graph layout) Linux CPG 625 MB vs OverflowDB 2,555 MB serialised, and Neo4j embedded used the most memory. So the layout matters, but a specialised compact layout beats both generic graph DBs and row stores.

findings.claim: On identical data and queries, specialised graph engines have not shown a decisive edge on lookups and 1 to 2 hop reads; relational systems often win or tie
findings.detail: GRADES 2017 (SF3/SF10, 32 cores, in memory): Postgres and Virtuoso SQL had the lowest latency on point lookups, 1-hop, 2-hop and single-pair shortest path; Neo4j Cypher comparable on reads; Gremlin layer cost up to 2 orders of magnitude; relational writes up to 10x faster. Old versions (Neo4j 2.3.6, PG 9.5). Kuzu CIDR 2023 (SF100): DuckDB won the 1-hop queries; Kuzu 5 to 20x faster than Umbra and 100x+ than DuckDB on selective multi-hop queries (IS02: Kuzu 16.7 ms, Umbra 189, DuckDB 5264), but Umbra/DuckDB win at 10 to 100 percent selectivity with Kuzu within 3.3x of best.

findings.claim: GRainDB: giving a plain columnar RDBMS graph-style joins closed most of the gap with a graph engine
findings.detail: Predefined joins (row-id CSR index + semijoin filters) cut DuckDB median time 3.6x on JOB and 22.5x on LDBC SNB, competitive with GraphflowDB; Neo4j community not competitive; index-nested-loop plans win with very selective filters, hash joins win on large many-to-many joins. Supports the owner's point that algorithms and data structure matter, and that an established relational engine with those additions is a real competitor.

findings.claim: A 2026 30-query n-hop benchmark on LDBC SF1-shaped data (3.18M nodes, 17.26M edges): DuckPGQ best geometric mean, Ladybug close, Neo4j and Kuzu slower
findings.detail: Apple M5, maintainer-run (a Ladybug-aligned author), custom 30 queries not official LDBC, Neo4j and FalkorDB in a Docker VM while others embedded, runs on different dates. Geometric mean vs Ladybug 0.21.2: DuckPGQ (DuckDB 1.5.6) 1.18x faster, Neo4j 2026.09 2.04x slower, Kuzu 1.76x slower, lance-graph 1.83x slower. Fastest on 13 (DuckPGQ), 10 (Ladybug), 5 (Neo4j), 1, 1 of 30. Q30 ms: Neo4j 1360, Kuzu 147, Ladybug 43.1, DuckPGQ 26.8, FalkorDB timeout (61.9 s). Q20: Neo4j 422, Kuzu 13.2, Ladybug 0.63, DuckPGQ 0.96, FalkorDB 0.46. Most queries tie within 1 to 5 ms. All engines passed the same 30 result assertions except FalkorDB (29).

findings.claim: Property-filtered variable-length path queries are poorly served by both families' stock engines; engine-specific early filtering is what matters
findings.detail: Rivera Correa and Riedewald (arXiv 2604.02553 v2, 2026-10-21): graphs 1.3k/78k to 13.1M/53.7M, lengths 2 to 10, Neo4j 5.24, Memgraph 3.5.1, Kuzu 0.11.2, DuckDB 1.4.1, unnamed commercial RDBMS. Both families materialise paths and check list constraints at the end. DuckDB without the paper's ReCAP beat the graph DBMSs on the regex-style query; Neo4j and Memgraph beat Kuzu at small lengths (index-free adjacency, Kuzu has a fixed cost tied to graph size); Kuzu memory reached 322 GB on one query at length 5; ReCAP reported up to 400,000x faster. Authors' own method, so treat the top speedups as best-case.

findings.claim: Where a graph structure makes a query cheap that a naive SQL formulation makes expensive: point-to-point shortest path with early stop, and large-frontier deep traversals; where SQL is competitive: bounded 1 to 3 hop reachability
findings.detail: MetaQA (43k entities, 135k triples; single author, hardware undisclosed, 2026-06-17): reachability p50 1/2/3 hops Postgres CTE 0.4/0.5/43.7 ms vs Neo4j 5.26 APOC BFS 2.9/2.3/171.5; shortest path at 4/5/6 hops Postgres BFS CTE 125/228/359 ms vs Neo4j shortestPath 1.5/1.9/2.7 ms (81x to 135x); all paths up to 4 hops Neo4j 28 ms vs Postgres 334 ms (p95 1.8 s). LOCAL (SQLite recursive CTE, covering index, 5 edges/node skewed): 1M nodes 5M edges: 3 hops 0.48 ms CTE vs 1.4 ms naive CSR (CSR pays an O(N) alloc); 4 hops 1.97 vs 1.38; 6 hops (22.6k reached) 46.3 ms CTE vs 2.57 ms CSR (18x). 100k nodes: 6 hops 22.7 vs 0.97 ms (23x); 10k nodes: 8.0 vs 0.28 ms (29x).

findings.claim: Recursive-CTE performance in DuckDB is improving fast; a 2026 vendor measurement shows 42.6x on reachability with unchanged SQL
findings.detail: 1M edges, 100k nodes, reachability CTE with UNION: median 4.051 s (1.5.5) to 0.095 s (2.0 preview); LDBC SF100 pathfinding 19.3 s to 2.95 s and 3.9 to 2.7 GB peak; 63-benchmark suite geomean +5.5 percent. Vendor-run, hardware not stated, measured on a preview not final 2.0.0. Suggests relational baselines should be rerun on 2.0.0 final, not quoted from older numbers.

findings.claim: Apache AGE variable-length edges are not a free win inside Postgres: they enumerate paths and lack BFS shortestPath
findings.detail: Issue 2349 (PG18.2, AGE 1.7.0, 100k nodes, 32 cores): [*1..3] count about 23 ms vs recursive CTE 0.34 ms, but the maintainer says the outputs differ (paths vs distinct nodes) and calls the combinatorial cost on dense cyclic graphs a real risk; allShortestPaths/shortestPath via BFS not implemented. The 10K and 100K timings being identical (23 ms) is odd and unverified.

findings.claim: Neo4j Community 2026.10.2 runs natively on Windows but is the heaviest option; ranking algorithms need the separate GDS library
findings.detail: Zip install, JDK 21 (or 25), neo4j console or windows-service; GPLv3 Community. GDS: in-memory projection required; Community GDS has all algorithms but a CPU cap per forum posts only, licence terms unconfirmed in official docs. Zip size not retrieved; Docker Hub latest listing 380 MB.

findings.claim: Memgraph, FalkorDB and Apache AGE are not native on Windows; using them adds a VM or Docker layer to the comparison
findings.detail: Memgraph: Docker or WSL (Docker Hub latest 744 MB; Community BSL, an OEM doc also names Apache 2.0, unresolved; MAGE 40+ algorithms). FalkorDB: Linux Docker image about 177 MB, FalkorDBLite embedded form supports Linux x64 and macOS arm64 only, Windows via WSL2; algorithms: BFS, SPpath, SSpath, A*, MSF, PageRank, betweenness, harmonic, WCC, CDLP, MaxFlow; GraphBLAS sparse-matrix storage. FalkorDB's own headline p99 (136 ms vs 46.9 s for Neo4j on Pokec) is vendor data and the multiple varies 344x to 500x across its pages.
findings.source: docs.falkordb.com/operations/falkordblite/falkordblite-ts; docs.falkordb.com/algorithms; Docker Hub tags; memgraph docs search results

findings.claim: CozoDB is effectively dormant; SurrealDB, TypeDB, Oxigraph and ArcadeDB are poor or unproven fits for this use
findings.detail: CozoDB last release v0.7.6 2023-12-11 (MPL-2.0, Datalog, PageRank/Dijkstra built in). SurrealDB: BSL, embedded Node engine package has a non-optional peer dependency and no verified Windows binary, no algorithm library seen. TypeDB 3.x Rust server, MPL-2.0, Windows build listed, no algorithms seen. Oxigraph: SPARQL, RocksDB, Apache/MIT, 'query evaluation not optimized yet'. ArcadeDB: Apache-2.0, ~monthly releases (26.7.3 July 2026), JVM 21, SQL/Cypher/Gremlin, claims 70+ algorithms (vendor), size and benchmark evidence not found.
findings.source: github.com/cozodb/cozo/releases; registry.npmjs.org/@surrealdb/node; github.com/oxigraph/oxigraph; github.com/ArcadeData/arcadedb; typedb search results

findings.claim: In-process libraries give the speed ceiling and the cheapest install for 10^3 to 10^6 nodes, but have no storage, no query language, and algorithm sets I did not enumerate
findings.detail: rustworkx 0.18.1 (2026-07-30, Apache-2.0, win wheel 2.3 MB), python-igraph 1.0.0 (2025-10-23, GPL, 3.2 MB), NetworkX 3.7 (2026-09-21, BSD-3, 2.1 MB, pure Python, Python 3.12+), graphology 0.26.0 (MIT, 2.7 MB unpacked, last npm publish about Jan 2025 inferred). A CSR with typed arrays held 5M edges in 24 MB and answered 6-hop reachability in 2.6 ms in my test (Node).
findings.source: PyPI and npm registry pages; local bench

findings.claim: Graph query languages cannot iterate algorithms such as PageRank; engines expose them as library calls, so 'ranking for free' only exists where an algo library is installed
findings.detail: arXiv 2601.06705 (2026-01-10) says Cypher/GQL/SQL-PGQ cannot express PageRank-style algorithms; recursive CTEs, libraries and vertex-centric APIs each miss expressiveness, performance or usability; proposes GraphAlg compiled to relational algebra (AvantGraph). A relational design can compute PageRank or degree once and store it as a column.

findings.claim: Code-analysis precedent: general-purpose graph databases were replaced by purpose-built stores in Joern; no evidence found for a generic property-graph DB beating a relational design on code-shaped graphs
findings.detail: Joern docs say older versions used general-purpose graph DBs with Gremlin and moved to its own in-memory OverflowDB, later flatgraph. Linux 4.1.16 CPG about 48M nodes, 431M edges. No benchmark found on import/call/test/doc-shaped graphs comparing graph vs relational engines, and none measuring tokens or answer quality. CodexGraph (NAACL 2025) reportedly cost 22k to 102k tokens per task (snippet only, not read).
findings.source: joern.readthedocs.io databaseOverview (snippet); flatgraph.joern.io/benchmarks; arxiv.org/abs/2408.03910 (fetched, no numbers)

findings.claim: LDBC audited results contain graph systems only; this shows what vendors submit, not that graph engines are faster than relational ones
findings.detail: Audited SNB Interactive entries 2024 to 2025 found: Huawei GES (2025-12-01, SF100/300/1000), GraphScope Flex (2025-04-21), Huawei with Cypher (2024-09). BI leaderboard top entries TigerGraph SF1000 (2024) and TuGraph SF30000 (2023). No audited relational entry surfaced in the search, and Umbra/DuckDB BI numbers were not found.

tables.title: Where each side wins, as supported by the sources
rows: Lookups and 1 to 2 hops on up to millions of edges: tie or relational slightly ahead (Pacaci 2017; Kuzu CIDR 2023; 2026 n-hop benchmark)
Reachability within 1 to 3 hops, bounded fan-out: recursive CTE with covering index is as fast as CSR (local test) and 4x faster than Neo4j APOC at 1 to 3 hops (MetaQA, single author)
Frontier in the tens of thousands (4 to 6+ hops): CSR 18x to 30x faster than recursive CTE (local test)
Point-to-point shortest path with early stop: graph engine 81x to 135x over a naive Postgres CTE BFS (MetaQA)
Selective filters + multi-hop joins: graph-style plans (Kuzu, GRainDB) 5x to 100x over plain DuckDB/Umbra plans; weak filters + big many-to-many: hash-join relational plans win (Kuzu CIDR, GRainDB)
Property-filtered variable-length paths: both families blow up on intermediates; only query-specific early filtering helps (arXiv 2604.02553)

All-paths enumeration returning path objects: graph engines natively return them; SQL needs path arrays; result size explodes on dense cyclic graphs in either (AGE issue; MetaQA all paths 28 ms vs 334 ms)
Ranking: no query language iterates PageRank; needs algo library (Ladybug algo, GDS, MAGE, DuckPGQ) or a stored column computed once in SQL

recommendations_for_the_build: Treat the data structure as the design variable: build the repo graph as typed nodes (file, symbol, test, doc, route, table) and typed edges (imports, calls, tests, documents, http-route-to-client-call, same-slice-across-runtime) with integer ids, and keep both a forward and reverse CSR. At 10^3 to 10^6 nodes a typed-array CSR in memory is 24 MB for 5M edges and answers 6-hop reachability in a few ms (local test), so the engine question is mostly about queries, ranking and persistence, not raw traversal.

Choose the engine contenders by fit: LadybugDB (embedded, CSR, Cypher with TRAIL/ACYCLIC/SHORTEST, algo extension) as the established-graph-engine arm; Neo4j Community 2026.10.2 as the reference native engine if a JVM server is acceptable; DuckDB 2.0 + DuckPGQ as the graph-flavoured relational arm. Skip Kuzu 0.11.3, CozoDB, AGE, Memgraph/FalkorDB (Docker/WSL on Windows), PostgreSQL SQL/PGQ (reverted).

Specialise to the repo: precompute per-edge-kind reverse adjacency, import-linter slice boundaries as edge attributes, cross-runtime edges from URL literal to route decorator, and cap hops by edge kind (imports unbounded with set semantics, calls 3 to 4, docs 1). Hop depth is a first-class parameter: report results at 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and unbounded because the winner changes with it.

Rank nodes once (in-degree, PageRank, or personalised PageRank from the query file) and store the score as a property so ranked retrieval is a lookup, not an iterative query. Verify Ladybug's algo extension installs on this PC before depending on it (needs network for INSTALL algo).
Use trail or acyclic semantics only when path objects are returned; for 'what depends on X' return a node set with set semantics so every engine can give an identical answer.
Pin versions and read the licences before choosing: LadybugDB changes quickly (0.19.1 in Aug to 0.22.3 in Nov 2026) and its file format is not guaranteed stable.
recommendations_for_the_test: Strongest relational arm: DuckDB 2.0.0 (recursive CTE with USING KEY, hash joins; also run DuckPGQ GRAPH_TABLE) and SQLite or PostgreSQL 18 as the production-shaped arm. Schema: typed node table and typed edge table with integer ids, composite primary key plus covering indexes in both directions (dst, kind, src) and (src, kind, dst), WITHOUT ROWID in SQLite. Traversal: level-wise BFS or recursive CTE with a depth cap and UNION (set semantics); path arrays only if paths are returned; bidirectional BFS from the application for point-to-point shortest path. Precompute closure or 'dependents within k' tables for hot files and store rank (degree, PageRank) as a column.

Graph arms: LadybugDB (embedded) and Neo4j Community 2026.10.2 (+ GDS only if ranking is tested), plus a typed-array CSR in memory as the ceiling. Tune each the way its docs recommend (Ladybug: indexes, ANALYZE, projected properties; Neo4j: indexes, warm cache) so no arm is a straw man.

Pin semantics before comparing answers: same output shape (node set vs path list), same direction, same depth cap, TRAIL or ACYCLIC vs set semantics stated, same tie rule for shortest paths. Check result equality on every query before timing; log mismatches as findings, not noise.

Score the answer, not only the latency: for each question, compare returned items to a ground-truth set built from an independent method (grep + import resolver + route-to-client match) and report precision, recall and rank quality, plus result size in tokens as the agent would receive it. Latency under about 10 ms is irrelevant against a 6.6 s model step.
Sweep hop depth 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and unbounded, and sweep fan-out (a hub file vs a leaf file), because published results flip with both. Report the reached-set size next to each time.

Use the EMS repo with its history (459 commits) so churn edges (co-change, fix commits) can be added as a relational and a graph edge kind; test incremental update cost per commit, not only read time. Rebuild from scratch and incrementally, and time both.

Measure on this PC with cold and warm caches, many sources per cell (30 or more), medians and p95, and record memory of each process. Run Neo4j with a fixed heap; do not compare a server in a VM with embedded engines without stating it (the 2026 benchmark did and said so).

Include a task-shaped query set from the repo's invariants in CLAUDE.md (e.g. what breaks if outbox sendOrQueue changes, which tests cover jobs/service.py transition, which clients regex the 409 detail string, which doc cites a file) and score each with the ground truth above.

HEAD graph (leaks edges added by the test commits) overstates hop 1: precision 0.435 at k=1. Truth files sit at hop 1: 33 %, hop 2: 34 %, hop 3: 15 %, hop 4: 2.5 %, unreached 15.6 %. Dependents-only (reverse imports): k=1 P 0.283 R 0.191; k=3 P 0.135 R 0.248; flat after; 26 % of queries have no dependent at all. Baselines: same directory (9.5 files) P 0.22 R 0.29; same slice name across runtimes (23.9 files) P 0.10 R 0.40.

findings.claim: Measured on this repo: PPR beats BFS order and co-change equals import-PPR, the combination has the highest point estimate, but intervals overlap at 45 test commits.
findings.detail: Ranked lists, split mode, P@10 (95 % bootstrap over commits): random 0.011 (0.006-0.016); most-imported files 0.067 (0.033-0.101); BFS 2 hops random tie-break 0.193 (0.162-0.223); PPR on imports restart 0.15 0.243 (0.197-0.285); PPR restart 0.30 0.237; PPR with symmetric degree normalisation 0.232 (0.194-0.268) so hub damping showed no gain; PPR on reverse edges only 0.104 (0.082-0.125); co-change confidence only (106 train commits) 0.259 (0.186-0.334); PPR imports + co-change weight 0.5 0.279 (0.226-0.332), weight 1.0 0.283 (0.225-0.342), weight 3.0 0.268. R@10 for the weight-1.0 hybrid 0.534 vs 0.454 for import PPR. All structured methods far above random and above the popularity baseline.

findings.claim: Measured on this repo: all 'unreached' co-changed pairs are cross-runtime, so an import graph has a recall ceiling near 85 % and cross-runtime typed edges are the only way to see the rest.
findings.detail: 1,028 co-changed pairs in the split-mode test set: 340 at hop 1, 348 at hop 2, 180 at hop 3+, 160 unreached. 158 of the 160 unreached pairs are cross-runtime (web/mobile/backend); cross-runtime pairs are 158 of 1,028 (15 %). Only about 40 of the 158 are in a same-named slice. Also 37 % of files changed in test commits are new files not in the graph at the split, and co-change on the HEAD file set covered only 46 % of queries because renames/deletes drop out (94 % in split mode), so rename tracking matters.

findings.claim: Measured: a full rebuild of the file-level import graph is about 0.4-0.5 s on this repo, so incremental update is not a performance need for that graph.
findings.detail: 5 runs, 0.40-0.49 s each, including git ls-files, git log and parsing 477 files (218 Python via ast, 259 JS/TS via regex) into adjacency. Cost that would grow is symbol/call resolution (language server or TypeScript compiler), not measured.

findings.claim: Change impact: richer static call graphs raise completeness but lower precision; the simplest graph gave the best balance.
findings.detail: 10 Java projects, about 17,000 mutants, truth = tests failing on the mutant. Graph sizes (nodes/edges): basic 48,571/106,105; +class hierarchy 48,571/114,660; +field analysis 62,153/175,512. Completeness gains about +20 % (simple to basic), +15 % (basic to hierarchy), +5 % (hierarchy to fields); precision falls as edges are added, hierarchy-graph precision 0.09 to 0.79 across cases. No per-hop table in the text read.
findings.source: Musco, Monperrus, Preux, Software Quality Journal 2017, arXiv 1812.06286 (ar5iv)

findings.claim: No published precision/recall-by-hop table for code impact analysis was found; 'precision collapses with hops' is expected but only measured here at file level.
findings.detail: Searched specifically; closest are a snippet that fixed-distance dynamic impact sets 'miss many further dependencies' and the small-agent finding that each extra hop multiplies localisation odds by 0.47-0.55. Treat as a gap.

findings.claim: Structural dependency is a weak predictor of co-change: most dependencies never carry a change, and many co-changes have no dependency path.
findings.detail: 35 Java projects: in most, more than half of dependencies never involved in propagation, few carry most events. 45 Java projects (Oliva and Gerosa): dependency raises co-change rate but classifiers built on it were often inaccurate. History-based heuristics beat call-graph ones in Hassan and Holt (secondary-source numbers, unverified).
findings.source: Geipel and Schweitzer 2009/TSE 2012; Oliva thesis; Hassan and Holt ICSM 2004 (search snippets)

findings.claim: Aider's repo map is personalised PageRank over a file graph with hub-damping multipliers, packed into a token budget by binary search; no ablation of the multipliers is published.
findings.detail: Edges referencing file to defining file per shared identifier; weight = multiplier x sqrt(reference count). Multipliers: x10 mentioned identifier, x10 long (8+) snake/camel names, x0.1 leading underscore, x0.1 if more than 5 definers, x50 if referencing file is a chat file; 0.1 self-loop for unreferenced definitions. Personalisation 100/num_files on chat files and name-matched files; nx.pagerank weighted. Packing: binary search on number of ranked tags until within 15 % of budget; default 1,024 tokens (x8 with no chat files, capped by context minus 4,096); per-file mtime tag cache. Blog post gives no measurements.

findings.claim: Graph expansion anchored on lexical matches improved localisation and cut tokens, but ablation deltas are modest and the best setting is a per-repo oracle.
findings.detail: LARGER: ablation on MuLocBench Acc@5 (full 55.7): no graph expansion 48.2, no confidence scoring 53.1, no community detection 53.4, none 46.8. LocBench Acc@5 87.0 (fixed) / 89.1 (tuned) vs Codex 74.1 and Claude Code 75.2 (different backbone). Tokens per instance 452K vs 591K and 353K vs 522K. Defaults k=10 top neighbours, edge confidence threshold 0.5; only 374 of 560 LocBench instances ran; hop-radius and sweep appendix not in the text read.

findings.claim: Hop radius for flat context: depth 1 helps, depth 2 can hurt; summarising 2-hop context recovers it.
findings.detail: RepoGraph on SWE-bench Lite (Agentless + GPT-4o): no graph 27.33 %; 1-hop flattened 2,310.7 tokens 29.67 %; 1-hop LLM-summarised 717.5 tokens 28.33 %; 2-hop flattened 10,505 tokens 26.00 %; 2-hop summarised 1,229 tokens 28.67 %. Only k=1,2 tested; k>=3 judged too noisy.

findings.claim: Multi-hop traversal beats 1-hop in an agent loop where the agent chooses hop count per call, but the effect is small.
findings.detail: LocAgent ablation (Qwen2.5-7B ft): full 88.32 file Acc@5 / 71.53 function Acc@10; hops fixed to 1: 86.86 / 66.79; no TraverseGraph 86.13 / 66.06; only contain relations 86.50 / 66.42; no SearchEntity 68.98 / 53.28; no BM25 index 75.18 / 60.22. Search is the dominant component, traversal second. Graph: directory/file/class/function nodes; contain/import/invoke/inherit edges; Python only.

findings.claim: Token cost of neighbourhood expansion grows steeply with depth; a depth cap of 4 on contain edges was needed to stay under 10k tokens per call.
findings.detail: SpIDER: input tokens for Python 2,642 at d=2 vs 29,658 at d=8; raising neighbour threshold N from 50 to 1000 raises 3,108 to 7,180. Negative results: TypeScript MRR@20 0.23 -> 0.08 with graph expansion; class-level Python MRR@20 0.36 vs 0.45 dense-only. Neighbourhood uses contain edges only.

findings.claim: Distance from the issue to the gold location drives success more than tool choice; graph tools help mainly at hop 0 and 1 and the advantage vanishes at 32B.
findings.detail: 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks: 186 at hop 0, 128 at hop 1, 78 at hop 2, 76 at hop 3+, 31 no mention. Each extra hop multiplies odds of correct localisation by 0.47-0.55 (four models), 0.50-0.67 across six Qwen3 sizes. Graph tools +8.1 points over grep for 4B (CI +3.0 to +13.5); embeddings -1.1; at 32B graph tool gain +2.0, p=0.27. Agents chained expansions in 12-14 % of episodes. 85 % of top-5 outputs were exact entity ids vs 47 % for grep; about half of the structured gain reflected id form. Calls were the edge type that connects most tasks (imports alone leave 12 tasks, inheritance alone 64 unreachable; from a search snippet). Resolution nearly conditional on correct localisation: 24-27 % vs 1-2 %.
findings.source: arXiv 2610.33958 (small coding agents and code graphs), html first half

findings.claim: LLM-driven multi-hop retrieval plateaus around 10 steps; the hop there is an iteration, not a radius.
findings.detail: DyRetriever (ASE 2026): swept 1-20, performance plateaued past 10 while tokens rose 19.1 %; removing multi-hop reasoning cut Pass@1 6.0-9.6 % relative and tokens 38-48 %. CoSIL: 10 iterations cap; pruning of rejected nodes worth 4 % relative; iteration sweep non-monotone.

findings.claim: A graph-navigation tool has value only if the agent calls it; one small study showed 42 % adoption and zero use on structural-chain tasks.
findings.detail: CodeCompass: 71-file repo, 255 edges (imports, inherits, instantiates), Neo4j, 1-hop tool, 30 authored tasks, 258 trials. Hidden-dependency group: 99.4 % vs about 76-78 % baselines; tool used in 42 % of trials, 0 of 30 structural-chain tasks. Validity risk: tasks designed around graph edges.

findings.claim: A tree-sitter graph server cut tokens about 10x at lower answer quality than a grep-and-read agent; it wins on graph-native questions and loses on source context and exhaustive call sites.
findings.detail: 31 repos (one per language), one model, grader was first author. Quality 0.83 vs 0.92; about 1,000 vs 10,000 tokens per question; 2.3 vs 4.8 tool calls; hub detection and caller ranking won in 19 of 31 languages; lost on full source context in 16 and exhaustive call-site search in 10; macro-heavy C 0.58 vs 1.00. No embedding or language-server baseline. Vendor-reported 99 % token cuts seen only as snippets and not used.
findings.source: arXiv 2603.27277 (abstract fetched); detail from fdeinterviews review (fetched, secondary)

findings.claim: History as edges: association rules give low recall and moderate precision, with a precision/recall trade-off set by support and confidence, and large change sets must be dropped.
findings.detail: ROSE, 8 projects: support 1, confidence 0.1 gives recall 0.15, precision 0.26, top-3 suggestions contain a correct location 64 %; support 3 / confidence 0.9 gives recall about 4 %, precision about 50 %; transactions touching more than 30 entities ignored. Evaluated per commit instead of pooled, a replication saw recall and precision about 20 % and 45 % lower (snippet). Tangled changes: 6-15 % of fixes (snippet). code-maat defaults min revs 5, min shared revs 5, min coupling 30 %, max change set 30; empty on small repos until lowered (snippet).
findings.source: Zimmermann et al. ICSE 2004/TSE 2005 (pdf text); Tosun and Romero 2019; Herzig and Zeller 2013; code-maat (snippets)

findings.claim: History length: recent commits are worth more than old ones; very short histories give the best precision on queries they can answer but answer few queries.
findings.detail: TARMAQ on 2 industrial and 17 open-source systems: applicability rises and levels off with history length, about 25,000 commits needed for acceptable applicability; MAP for applicable queries highest for very short histories; age zero best, model should be rebuilt as it ages. On this repo (106 usable training commits) co-change still ranked as well as the import graph (P@10 0.259 vs 0.243, overlapping intervals) with 94 % of seeds having any train link, but the history is bursty and single-team.
findings.source: Moonen, Di Alesio, Rolfsnes, Binkley, history length and age (Simula pdf text); impact_vs_hops.py

findings.claim: Test selection: class (file) level static selection is nearly as safe and fast as dynamic; method-level call-graph selection is less safe, less precise and slower than running everything.
findings.detail: 22 projects, 985 revisions. Share of tests selected: Ekstazi 20.6 %, class-level static 29.4 %, method-level 43.8 %. Revisions with safety violations vs Ekstazi: class-level 0.2 % (2 of 22 projects), method-level 10.6 % (14 projects); precision violations 33.0 % vs 55.7 %. End-to-end time vs retest-all: class-level static 62.5-65 %, Ekstazi 64-68 %, method-level 695 % average. Unsafe cases from reflection and library exclusion.
findings.source: Legunsen et al. FSE 2016 (pdf text, Tables 2-3)

findings.claim: Transitive dependency selection selects tests of which about 99.9 % pass; a learned selector uses history features and dependency distance.
findings.detail: Meta predictive test selection: catches over 99.9 % of faulty changes and over 95 % of failures with fewer than a third of tests, gradient-boosted trees. Feature importance ratios (classification/ranking): historical failure rate 1.37/1.62, file change history 1.03/1.59, minimal dependency distance 1.23/0.96, common path tokens 0.33/0.68, distinct authors 0.3/0.72. TDAD (graph with CALLS/IMPORTS/TESTS, confidence 1.0 direct test, 0.56 transitive, 0.45 imports) cut test-level regression 6.08 % to 1.82 % on 100 instances but reported no selection precision/recall, lowered resolution 31 % to 29 %, and a TDD prompt alone raised regressions to 9.94 %.

findings.claim: Natural-language summaries of code are far worse than code or signatures as model input; compact structural context cuts tokens without losing resolves.
findings.detail: Oracle localisation, SWE-bench Verified: summaries answered 4 of 45 behavioural questions vs 27 of 45 for source (a frontier model's summaries no better than a 3B model's). UML skeletons/signatures for the rest of a file resolved no more than deleting it (N=70, p=0.75). Compressed context matched whole files at about a third of tokens (about 19K vs 94K per resolved issue). About 9 % of outcomes flipped between identical temperature-0 runs. Per-representation figures (signature+docstring 6/45) from a secondary blog, unverified.

findings.claim: Availability of the facts an edit depends on decides success; distance does not; a stale convention document costs more than none.
findings.detail: Seven models, five harnesses, synthetic migrations: supplied facts work as well far from the edit as beside it; harnesses that all pass differ more than tenfold in tokens. Implication for graph edges to docs: a doc edge to a stale document is a hazard.

findings.claim: Community detection: Leiden fixes Louvain's disconnected communities; evidence that community summaries help an agent is one small ablation.
findings.detail: Louvain: up to 25 % badly connected, up to 16 % disconnected communities; Leiden guarantees connected communities and is faster (snippet). LARGER: removing community priors cost 4.1 % relative on one benchmark. No study found of community summaries improving agent answers. Inference: this repo already declares 12 slices as same-named folders under import-linter contracts, so detection mostly rediscovers declared structure.

findings.claim: Freshness: published systems update per file (mtime, changed-file re-parse, per-file stack graphs, stacked immutable databases); none reports a rebuild-versus-incremental comparison.
findings.detail: Aider tag cache keyed by mtime (read); LARGER re-parses only changed files per commit (read); GitHub stack graphs file-incremental (snippet, arXiv 2211.01224); Meta Glean indexes O(fanout of change) with stacked immutable databases (snippet, 2024-12-19). How change is detected (hash vs time) was not in the material read.
findings.source: aider repomap.py; arXiv 2605.16352; GitHub stack graphs; Meta Glean blog

findings.claim: Static Python call graphs miss about 30 % of real edges; no JS/TS figure was retrieved.
findings.detail: PyCG: about 99.2 % precision, about 69.9 % recall (authors' own benchmarks). The repo is 218 Python and 259 JS/TS code files.

recommendations_for_the_build: Q1 'what could break if I change this': directed reverse reachability (dependents) with an explicit depth cap, shown in tiers by hop, ranked by personalised PageRank seeded on the changed files. Do not return the undirected closure (measured: a quarter of the repo by hop 6, versus about 2 % for directed dependents). Keep a separate 'edited together before' list from co-change rather than mixing it into the dependency tier. Hop limit 2 with a visible count of what lies beyond; sweep 1 to 4.

Q1 edge types in expected order of value: import (test files as importers), test-to-source, route-to-client-call and same-named slice (the cross-runtime edges are the only way to see the 15 % of co-changed pairs that imports cannot reach), co-change, migration-to-model; docs-citing-file as a separate list because a stale doc is worse than none. Output per item: path, kind, hop, one-line signature of the linking symbol; path only for the long tail.

Q1 tests: select at file/class level with the project's own import and mock links; avoid method-level call-graph selection (less safe, less precise, slower than running everything in the measured study). For a hub changed file such as backend/app/core/db.py, report that it selects everything and fall back to the slice's tests. Learned weighting by failure and change history is the strongest published feature but needs test-outcome history.

Q2 'what do I need to read to do this task': lexical or symbol anchors from the task text, aligned to graph nodes, then personalised PageRank (restart 0.15 to 0.30) from the anchors over imports + calls + co-change edges, packed into the token budget by binary search on entry count (Aider design). Default expansion 1 hop; let the agent ask for a second expansion rather than widening the radius. Output: ranked paths, signature lines for the top few, path only for the rest, full source only for files the agent opens. No natural-language summaries of code.

Q3 'where is the thing that does X': symbol and lexical index first (the largest ablation effect in the literature is the search component), graph only to expand and rerank at 1 hop. Return fully qualified ids (path plus symbol) plus signature in the exact form the agent will use next; id form alone explained about half the structured gain in one study. Edges: defined-in, import, same-named slice, route string to handler.

Co-change edges: build from non-merge commits on main, drop change sets over 30 code files, track renames (git log --follow or -M) because the HEAD file set lost over half the co-change coverage, weight recent commits more, rebuild on each merge. Treat minimum support (1, 2, 3) and the tangled-commit filter as parameters.

Do not spend effort on hub damping, transitive reduction, dominators or community detection first: hub damping showed no gain here, no empirical study of reduction/dominators for impact sets was found, and the 12 slices are already declared. Leiden is worth a later test only where it disagrees with the declared slices.
Freshness: rebuild the file-level graph on demand (about 0.4 to 0.5 s here). Store a content hash per node only to validate a cached symbol-level layer, which is the part that will cost more.
recommendations_for_the_test: Score both stores on the same ground truth and report value per token, not store size: (a) files co-changed in historical commits with a time split and a leak-free graph rebuilt at the split commit (the HEAD graph leaks the test commits' own new imports and overstated hop-1 precision 0.435 vs 0.315), (b) tests that fail on historical or injected changes, (c) files an agent actually opens and edits in real tasks.

Report precision and recall at fixed list sizes (5, 10, 20) and at fixed token budgets, with 95 % intervals that resample commits (queries inside a commit share truth). With 45 test commits the differences between PPR, co-change and the hybrid were inside the noise; use more history, or all-refs, or several time splits (rolling origin) before claiming a winner.

Include cheap non-graph baselines in every comparison: same directory, same slice name, grep plus names, most-imported files, random. In this repo same-directory (P 0.22 as a set) is not far behind a 1-hop import set (P 0.315).

Sweep these parameters: hop radius 1 to 4 and uncapped directed closure; direction (undirected, dependents-only, dependencies-only); ranking (BFS, PPR restart 0.10/0.15/0.30, degree-normalised, Aider-style multipliers); edge set (imports, +tests, +route-to-client, +co-change weight 0.5/1/3, +same-slice, +docs); history window (last 50, 100, all), recency decay, min support 1/2/3, change-set cap 15/30, rename tracking on/off, tangled filter on/off; token budget 500/1,000/2,000/4,000; output form (paths, path+signature, snippet, summary); Leiden prior on/off; rebuild vs hash-validated reuse.

Hold out evaluation tasks from anything used to tune the graph (LARGER's tuned setting is a per-repo oracle; CodeCompass's tasks were built around graph edges). Measure tool adoption: a graph the agent does not call carries no value (42 % adoption, 0 of 30 structural tasks in one study).

Add a symbol-level call-resolution arm (TypeScript compiler for JS/TS, ast for Python) and a route-to-client edge arm and measure them against the file-level import arm on the same queries; the current experiment only measures file-level imports and cannot say what call edges add. Expect Python call recall around 70 % (PyCG).
open_questions: How much do symbol-level call edges and route-to-client edges add over file-level imports on this repo? Only the file-level import graph was built; the cross-runtime gap is counted (158 of 1,028 pairs) not filled.
Is the PPR-over-BFS and hybrid-over-either difference real? Intervals overlap with 45 test commits; needs more commits, several rolling time splits, or the all-refs history (459 commits).

Does 'edited together' (commit co-change) track 'would break'? Test-failure ground truth was not used here; the literature ground truths (Musco mutants, Meta test failures) differ from commit co-change.

What is the right unit for the dependents tier on hubs such as core/db.py (43 importers)? No evidence found for hub-specific handling beyond Aider's x0.1 multiplier for identifiers with more than 5 definers, which has no published ablation.

Do signatures beat paths-only for this repo's agents? The one controlled study (Python, SWE-bench) found skeletons no better than deleting the rest of the file (p 0.75) and summaries much worse; the coding sessions that wrote this product are not on this machine.
Does tool adoption depend on prompt design? CodeCompass found 42 % overall and 0 of 30 on structural-chain tasks; the delivery form (MCP tool, pre-injected map, hook) was not compared.
not_covered: Hop-depth precision/recall tables for call-graph impact analysis on real code: not found in the literature and not measured at call level here.
Symbol-level call graph, route-to-client edges, and test-failure ground truth for this repo: not built or measured.

research.lane: production code-intelligence systems: stores, query languages, reasons; and fair-comparison method for graph vs relational (researched 2026-11-12)

findings.claim: CodeQL uses a relational data model on its own Datalog engine, and its authors say off-the-shelf SQL performed badly for their queries.
findings.detail: QL compiles to Datalog and runs on relational tables (one per language construct). ECOOP 2016 footnote 5: early compiler translated QL to SQL on a third-party DB; 'Performance was disappointing, since typical QL compiles to very complex SQL with deeply nested joins and lots of recursion. Most SQL systems are not designed with such queries in mind'. They built a custom engine (no updates or transactions needed) with inlining, join ordering and magic sets. This is evidence against a naive SQL engine for deep recursive joins, and also against a general graph DB: the model stayed relational.
findings.source: Avgustinov, de Moor, Peyton Jones, Schaefer, 'QL: Object-oriented Queries on Relational Data', ECOOP 2016 (local text: research/production/txt/ql_ecoop2016.txt); CodeQL docs 'About CodeQL' (undated)

findings.claim: Joern moved from general-purpose graph databases to a purpose-built in-process graph store (OverflowDB, then flatgraph); results are mixed by query type and self-published.
findings.detail: docs.joern.io: older versions used general-purpose graph DBs plus Gremlin, now parallel low-memory graph APIs. Joern team JMH benchmarks (16 Defects4J projects, 8 GB heap): Neo4j timed out on writes from a mid-size project on and used the most memory; TinkerGraph trailed OverflowDB/flatgraph on most; but on multi-hop AST traversals (astDFS, astUp) TinkerGraph and Neo4j beat OverflowDB until large projects. flatgraph read speed gain over OverflowDB 50% to >99.5%, 25-30% less memory; Linux 4.1.16 CPG 625 MB vs 2,555 MB, 11.97 vs 18.18 min. flatgraph README: ~259 bytes/node in memory, ~36.6 B/node on disk on an ad hoc schema. The store is a custom adjacency structure, not a graph DBMS. 2014 Neo4j origin is from a snippet.

findings.claim: Glean is a fact store (RocksDB, typed immutable facts, Datalog-like Angle) and its stated reason is generality, not a verdict on graph or relational DBs.
findings.detail: Facts form a DAG, predicates ~ tables, stacked immutable databases for incremental indexing, derived predicates ~ materialised views, Angle currently non-recursive. Lookup by qualified name about 1 ms. The Meta post gives no comparison to graph or relational stores and no dataset size figures.
findings.source: Meta engineering 'Indexing code at scale with Glean'; glean.software/docs/introduction

findings.claim: Glean beat a SQLite-based index (hiedb) on size and speed, but the relational side lacked a name index and held possibly more data.
findings.detail: Full Hackage, GHC 9.4.7: hiedb 5.2 GB and 1021 s to index vs Glean 0.8 GB and 470 s. Find references to one name: hiedb 2.3 s (full table scan in name-refs), Glean 0.39 s via Glass, 0.03 s raw. findings.claim: Kythe defines a graph schema but serves from denormalised tables; stack graphs use a graph with a constrained path algorithm for name binding.
findings.detail: Kythe: nodes (VNames), edges (ref, defines/binding, childof, extends, overrides, typed), facts; storage doc says general graph query performance is not a priority and data is converted to 'denormalized paged association tables, or graph-database triples' for serving, reverse edges generated at serving. Stack graphs: per-file graphs built in isolation, merged at query time, name resolution is path finding with a symbol stack and edge precedence; reasons: incremental at GitHub scale, zero config, per-language declarative rules. findings.claim: Unweighted dependency closure over-selects; Meta replaced it with a learned model, and file-level granularity can beat finer or coarser choices on cost.
findings.detail: Meta: build-dependency selection says 'impacted' more often than necessary, up to a quarter of all tests per change on mobile; model (gradient-boosted tree on history) catches >99.9% of regressions running about a third of tests that transitively depend on the change; paper: cost halved, >95% failing tests caught. Ekstazi (snippet): file-level chosen over method-level for overhead; Ekstazi# file-level cut test methods 75.6% vs module-level.

findings.claim: The 2026 agent-era graph tool Codebase-Memory stores its property graph in one SQLite file and traverses by recursive CTE.
findings.detail: arXiv 2603.27277 (2026-03-28): typed nodes and edges (CALLS, HTTP_CALLS, IMPORTS, TESTS, FILE_CHANGES_WITH...), BFS via SQL recursive CTE about 0.3 ms at depth 5, configurable depth, Louvain communities, 100,000-row ceiling, no ranking algorithm described. Eval: 31 repos (78 to 49,398 nodes), quality 0.83 vs 0.92 for a grep-and-read agent, about 1,000 vs 10,000 tokens per question, 2.3 vs 4.8 tool calls; first author graded, no blinding mentioned; no relational baseline. Explorer agent won where full source or exhaustive grep mattered.

findings.detail: sverklo post: 60 tasks, 2 repos; smart grep F1 0.67 / 731 tokens / 11.8 calls; sverklo F1 0.58 / 255 tokens / 1.0 call; naive grep F1 0.35 / 15,814 tokens; cold start (3.7 s) excluded; dead-code F1 0.02. Other 2026 claims (CodeGraph 51-64%, grepai 97%, 62x-120x token cuts) are search snippets from vendor or author posts, unverified. findings.source: dev.to/nike-17 benchmark post (undated); aider.chat/2023/10/22/repomap.html; search snippets

findings.claim: Careful graph-vs-relational benchmarks fix the data, the queries and the declared schema, include indexes as part of the schema, validate result equality, and split query classes (LDBC).
findings.detail: LDBC SNB spec v2.2.2: any language or API allowed; relational systems explicitly in scope; schema includes every index, materialised view and non-default setting and must be identical across runs; explicit auxiliary structures counted as schema; validation step compares results to a reference; audited with a full disclosure report; BI workload has 38 choke points in 9 categories including path finding and path cardinality estimation; 2-3 hop patterns reward indexes but cause scattered accesses.
findings.source: LDBC Social Network Benchmark specification v2.2.2, arXiv 2001.02299v9 (local text: txt/ldbc_snb.txt)

findings.claim: A relational system through a Gremlin-to-SQL layer was slowest at BFS depth 3+ and shortest path, but among the fastest at 1-2 hop single-label queries and property search.
findings.detail: Lissandrini et al. microbenchmarks: same Gremlin queries on all systems, same random start nodes, vendor-recommended settings, 24-core 128 GB host, 2 h timeouts, BFS depth 2-5. Neo4j 3.0 best BFS at all depths; OrientDB and Titan next; Sqlg (Postgres 9.6, one table per vertex type, one join table per edge label) slowest for depth >=3 and shortest path ('accesses all tables for all edges, and performs very large joins'). Authors: with mostly property search and few traversals prefer hybrid/relational; with heterogeneous edge types and traversals prefer native. Caveat: translation layer, not tuned recursive SQL; forced Gremlin.
findings.source: Lissandrini, Brugnara, Velegrakis, 'Beyond Macrobenchmarks', PVLDB 12(4) (local text: txt/lissandrini2018.txt)

findings.claim: Tuning alone moves relational traversal times by 10x to 80x, so an untuned relational baseline is not a fair comparison.
findings.detail: Hohenstein and Jergler (PostgreSQL 9.5, laptop, 500K nodes x 50 edges and 5M nodes x 4): index on edge table took warm PATHS(5) from about 60 s to 6.4 s; LIMIT 1 in EXISTS sub-queries 4.54 s to 0.057 s; cache 128 MB to 1 GB 4.54 s to 0.46 s (cold barely changed); array columns halved ALL(4) at the cost of 1NF; JDBC fetch size 1 to 1000 took 30 s to 18 s; ALL(9) 8.0 s and ALL(10) 26.4 s warm on 5M nodes. Similar-sounding scenarios differ by about 1000x. Their list of unfairness: overgeneralising one product, small in-memory data, warm starts, default config, over-tuning one query, synthetic scenarios, naive schemas or mismatched languages, data distribution and fan-out, aggregated scores.
findings.source: Hohenstein and Jergler, 'Database Performance Comparisons: An Inspection of Fairness', DATA 2019

findings.claim: Headline graph-over-relational multipliers come from untuned or vendor-run setups.
findings.detail: Neo4j-in-Action table (snippet of Neo4j's page, which returned 404): 1,000 users, depth 4, MySQL 1,543.5 s vs Neo4j 1.359 s, MySQL fails at depth 5; Hohenstein's Postgres tests contradict the pattern. Survey (Suzumura et al., 2021): Vicknair 2010 found MySQL and Neo4j similar up to 100K nodes with structural queries faster in Neo4j; Wycislik found Oracle faster on local clustering coefficient; TigerGraph's own report 4x-100x over Neo4j/Titan is vendor-run. Relational-side research claims (SQLGraph SIGMOD 2015: 2-8x over Titan, Neo4j, OrientDB; Grail CIDR 2015) are also authors' own and snippet-only.
findings.source: neo4j.com news post (snippet); arXiv 2005.12873v4 (local text); SQLGraph and Grail snippets

findings.claim: Naive recursive SQL is the usual cause of slow relational traversal and is fixable with visited-set semantics.
findings.detail: DuckDB USING KEY post (2025-05-23): vanilla recursive CTE keeps all intermediate rows; shortest path on a 424-node, 1,446-edge graph processed 605,859,791 rows (text says nearly 1 billion, table says 605.9M) vs 19,213 with USING KEY. SQLite docs: UNION (not UNION ALL) drops duplicates and ends cycles; indexes on both edge columns help; ORDER BY plus LIMIT in the recursive select makes a priority queue; LIMIT always stops recursion.

findings.claim: Standard SQL graph syntax is not a safe dependency: Postgres 19 SQL/PGQ appears to have been rolled back, and the best embedded graph engine (Kuzu) was archived.
findings.detail: SQL/PGQ committed 2026-03-16, rewritten to ordinary joins, no variable-length paths in the listed features; depesz page notes rollback; PostgreSQL 19 RC1 release notes (as of 2026-10-09) do not mention it; DevX (snippet) says reverted in beta 4. DuckPGQ is an experimental DuckDB extension. Kuzu repo archived 2025-10-10 (last release 0.11.3); forks Ladybug (0.17.1, June 2026) and RyuGraph continue it; Apple acquisition reported by heise but unconfirmed (snippets).
findings.source: depesz.com 2026-07-31 post; postgresql.org/docs/19/release-19.html; The Register 2025-10-14, oneuptime 2026-08-12 (snippets)

findings.claim: Engine choice cannot change the answer set for identical edges and queries; value differences come from content, algorithm and output shaping.
findings.detail: Inference from the sources: LDBC validates equal results across engines; production systems (Kythe, SCIP, Codebase-Memory) hold the same logical graph in tables or flat records; ranking (Aider), distance cutoffs (Google), learned weights (Meta) and typed cross-file edges are what change what an agent receives. At this repo's scale (my estimate: file graph hundreds to low thousands of nodes, symbol graph tens of thousands) every engine answers in milliseconds (Codebase-Memory: ~0.3 ms depth-5 BFS on up to 49K nodes), so engine speed is not where a graph can win.
findings.source: synthesis of LDBC spec, Codebase-Memory, TAP, Meta PTS, Aider

recommendations_for_the_build: Build one typed edge list first (file, symbol, route, doc, test, import-linter contract, cross-runtime HTTP edges, git co-change) and load it into every candidate store; a property graph is two tables, so make the table form the shared source of truth.

Strong relational baseline: integer ids and dictionary-encoded kinds; tables file, symbol, edge(src,dst,kind,weight,evidence_file,line), route, doc_ref, cochange, edge_unresolved (raw plus resolved); covering indexes (src,kind,dst) and (dst,kind,src); index symbol(name) plus a lower-cased or FTS5 copy; WITHOUT ROWID or clustered; STRICT tables; ANALYZE; WAL; check every query with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN for scans.

Write recursion correctly: UNION for a visited set (SQLite) or DuckDB USING KEY; depth column with a WHERE depth < k bound; MIN(depth) per node; ORDER BY plus LIMIT inside the recursive select for top-N; do not enumerate paths unless paths are the answer.

Precompute a bounded closure table reach(src,dst,dist) up to the calibrated k, refreshed per file on content_hash change (Glean derived-predicate and stack-graph per-unit style), so k-hop queries become index lookups.

Put answer shaping in the store for both sides: per-file and per-symbol cards (signature lines, SCIP and Aider style), a ranking column (distance, in-degree, co-change weight), and a token-budgeted top-N output. Without this the relational side is handicapped on the owner's actual objective.

Graph-side algorithms worth building on an in-memory adjacency projection (CSR arrays built from the table, the Joern pattern) rather than a graph DBMS: personalised ranking, bounded k-shortest or label-sequence constrained paths (route to handler to service to repository), co-change-weighted proximity, community detection. These are the places a graph can add value that tables do not give for free.

Calibrate hop depth and edge weights from this repo's history before the test, as Google did: measure graph distance between files that actually changed together in the 72 fix commits and the other commits; freeze k and weights, then compare.

Treat Kuzu forks (Ladybug, RyuGraph), DuckDB with DuckPGQ, and Neo4j as optional engine candidates only; Postgres 19 SQL/PGQ should not be assumed. Install sizes were not checked. Anything installed needs the owner's decision.
Include a granularity ablation (file-level vs symbol-level edges): Ekstazi, Nx and Turborepo show coarse can be cost-effective and Meta shows unweighted closure over-selects.
recommendations_for_the_test: Same edge set in every store; verify identical result sets for identical queries (LDBC validation step) before scoring anything; report any mismatch (Marlow's 416 vs 415 shows how it slips).

Declare the schema and every index, materialised view and setting for each store, as LDBC does; give each candidate comparable tuning effort and document it; run EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on the relational side and show no scans.

Query classes by hop depth, reported separately, never averaged: name lookup; k=1 neighbours; k=2, 3, 5 bounded reverse reachability; unbounded closure; one shortest path; label-sequence constrained path across runtimes; ranked top-N under a token budget. Include both directions (dependents and dependencies).
Report cold and warm runs, index and build time, file size per unit of information content (say what each store holds), memory, and incremental update cost for a one-file change.
Add a scale-up arm (synthetic replication of the edge list or a larger real monorepo) to find where native adjacency starts to win; at this repo's size no engine difference is expected to show.

Score value, not time or size: ground-truth relevant sets from git history (files co-changed in fix commits, test files touched together, doc-code pairs), recall and precision at fixed token budgets, tokens per correct answer, tool calls per task. Keep the grader independent of the system builder (Codebase-Memory and sverklo were graded by their authors).
Give the relational baseline the same ranking and card layer as the graph candidate, or the test measures the ranking rather than the store.

Include a tuned grep and file-read baseline (sverklo post: tuned grep had higher F1 than the graph server) and hybrid configurations; Codebase-Memory found the graph complemented rather than replaced exploration.
State and keep fixed: cutoff k, row ceilings (Codebase-Memory used 100,000), timeouts, and how timeouts or truncated results are counted.
